units.title: The Endocrine System
units.intro:
**Exocrine** glands have ducts (sweat, saliva). **Endocrine** glands are ductless — hormones go straight into blood and hunt a *target organ*. Compared with nerves: hormones are slower and last longer (growth, metabolism, cycles).

A gland fires when nerves poke it, or when another hormone pokes it (the pituitary is the usual “boss”).

The Endocrine Glands
body: Tap a gland on the figure to see what it secretes.

The main endocrine glands are the **hypothalamus** and **pituitary** (in the head; the pituitary is the "master gland" that controls other glands), the **thyroid** and **parathyroids** (neck), the **thymus** (chest), the **adrenal glands** (on top of the kidneys), the **islets of Langerhans** in the pancreas, and the **gonads** — ovaries and testes.
Endocrine glands are ductless: they release hormones straight into the blood, which carries them to target organs.

cards.title: 1.1.1 The Pituitary Gland
body: The pituitary gland is a small, bean-shaped gland located in the lower part of the brain.
The pituitary gland is structurally and functionally divided into two major lobes.
The growth hormone (GH), or somatotropic hormone, promotes normal skeletal and muscular growth by regulating cell division, protein synthesis, and bone growth.
Prolactin causes the mammary glands in breasts to develop and produce milk in women who are breastfeeding.

cards.title: 1.1.2 The Thyroid Gland
body: The human thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped gland, located at the base of the neck in front of the trachea (windpipe).
The thyroid gland is critical to the healthy development and maturation of vertebrates, and regulates metabolism.
The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine and calcitonin hormones.
Iodine is an essential component of thyroxine, and its synthesis requires iodine to be present in the diet.

cards.title: 1.1.3 The Parathyroid Glands
body: Parathyroid (para – meaning beside) glands are usually four small, flattened glands which are located behind the thyroid gland.
The parathyroid glands secrete a parathyroid hormone (PTH), or parathormone, that controls the concentration of calcium ions in the blood.
The correct amounts of calcium ions in the bloodstream are necessary for muscle contraction, nerve impulse transmission, bone and teeth development, blood clotting and other tasks.
When the concentration of calcium ions in the blood decreases, PTH activates bone cells to release calcium and phosphate ions, and stimulates the kidneys to conserve them.

cards.title: 1.1.4 The Adrenal Glands
body: The adrenal cortex is the bulky, outer portion of the gland and secretes many steroid hormones, collectively known as corticosteroids, or corticoids.
Corticosteroids fall into three categories: glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids.
Glucocorticoids regulate metabolism (fat and protein), help the body adapt to stress, and repair damaged tissues.
One of the most important glucocorticoid hormones is cortisol, which increases the metabolic rate of fats, proteins and carbohydrates.

cards.title: 1.1.5 The Pancreas
body: Exocrine cells secrete digestive juices or pancreatic juices.
Scattered through the pancreas are groups of endocrine cells called the islets of Langerhans.
The islets of Langerhans constantly monitor the amount of glucose in the blood.
Insulin triggers the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen.

cards.title: 1.1.6 The Sex Glands
body: Gamete production also takes place in these sex glands.
The human reproductive system consists of a pair of primary reproductive organs (gonads), accessory glands and ducts.
The male has two oval gonads, called testes, and the female has two gonads, called ovaries.
The testes contain endocrine tissue referred to as Leydig cells (interstitial cells).

cards.title: 1.1.7 The Thymus Gland
body: The size of the thymus varies considerably from person to person; however, the thymus gland is relatively large in newborns and children, and sharply decreases in size after puberty.
In adults, the gland gradually degenerates (shrinks) until it almost disappears.
The thymus gland therefore is functional primarily in childhood.
White blood cells multiply, differentiate and mature in this gland.

cards.title: 1.1.8 The Pineal gland
body: The pineal (“pinealis” meaning “shaped like a pine cone”) gland is a small mass; a cone-shaped tissue located in the brain.
The pineal gland contains cells that are light sensitive (photosensitive).
The blood levels of melatonin therefore vary from day to night, and they also change according to the season (spring, summer, autumn, winter).
Melatonin controls skin pigmentation (colour).

cards.problem: Which of the following describes the mechanism of secretion of an endocrine gland compared to an exocrine gland?

steps.text: **Step 1: Understand gland anatomy**
Endocrine glands are ductless glands that release their secretions, called hormones, directly into the surrounding interstitial fluid and blood vessels.
Exocrine glands, such as sweat and salivary glands, possess ducts that carry their secretions to a body surface or cavity.
**Step 2: Evaluate options**
The option correctly specifying that endocrine glands secrete directly into the bloodstream and exocrine glands use ducts is the accurate description.

cards.answer: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, whereas exocrine glands secrete substances through ducts.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Hormone target specificity is determined by which of the following cellular features?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define hormone-receptor binding**
Hormones circulate throughout the entire body via the blood, but only affect cells that express specific protein receptors that can bind that hormone.
**Step 2: Relate to cell characteristics**
Cells without these specialized receptors are blind to the hormonal signal, making receptor presence the key factor in specificity.
**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.answer: The presence of unique protein receptors on or inside the target cell

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following hormones is synthesized by neurosecretory cells in the hypothalamus but released by the posterior pituitary?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify posterior pituitary physiology**
The posterior pituitary gland does not synthesize its own hormones. It stores and secretes hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.

**Step 2: Recognize the specific hormones**
These hormones are oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone ($$ADH$$, also known as vasopressin).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Antidiuretic Hormone ($$ADH$$)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone directly stimulates the development of ovarian follicles in females and sperm production in males?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Review gonadotropic hormones**
$$FSH$$ and $$LH$$ are gonadotropic hormones from the anterior pituitary that regulate reproductive functions.

**Step 2: Define specific role of FSH**
$$FSH$$ stimulates follicle growth in females and spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules of males.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Follicle-Stimulating Hormone ($$FSH$$)**.

cards.title: Disorders of the endocrine glands
body: **Too little growth hormone** in childhood → dwarfism; **too much** → gigantism. **Lack of iodine** → goitre. **Too little insulin** (or cells not responding) → **diabetes mellitus (high blood glucose). **Too much thyroxine** → overactive thyroid (fast heartbeat, weight loss); **too little** in children → stunted growth and slow mental development.

questions.q: A group of Grade 11 students in Asmara are classifying the glands of the human body according to how their secretions leave the gland. Which ONE of the following structures is classified as an endocrine gland?

options.D: Digestive gland opening into the small intestine

why: **Recall the defining structural feature.** The unit defines endocrine glands as entirely ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream or surrounding interstitial fluid, using a rich capillary network rather than a duct.

**Recall the defining feature of exocrine glands.** Exocrine glands synthesize secretions that are channelled through anatomical ducts directly to an epithelial surface. Sweat glands, salivary glands and digestive organs are named in the unit as exocrine examples.

**Test each option in turn.** B (sweat gland) and C (salivary gland) deliver their secretions through ducts onto the skin and into the mouth respectively, and D (digestive gland) delivers digestive secretion through a duct into the intestinal lumen; all three are therefore exocrine. The thyroid gland has no duct and releases its hormones, such as thyroxine, into the blood.
**Conclude.** Only the thyroid gland is ductless and blood-borne in its secretion, so it is the only endocrine structure listed.

questions.q: Which ONE of the following glands releases its secretion through an anatomical duct onto an epithelial surface?
why: **State the criterion.** A gland whose product travels along an anatomical duct to an epithelial surface is by definition an exocrine gland.

**Check the options.** The anterior pituitary (A), the parathyroid gland (B) and the adrenal cortex (D) are all ductless endocrine tissues that pour their hormones into the blood. The salivary gland pours saliva along a duct into the mouth.
**Conclude.** Only the salivary gland uses a duct, so it is the exocrine gland required.

questions.q: A gland in the neck of a patient in Keren is found to possess an extremely rich capillary network but no excretory duct of any kind. State, with a reason, whether this gland is endocrine or exocrine.
questions.answer: The gland is endocrine, because it is ductless and its dense capillary network allows its hormonal product to diffuse directly into the bloodstream.
why: **Use the two structural criteria given.** The unit distinguishes the two gland types by the presence or absence of ducts and by the route the secretion takes: ducts to an epithelial surface for exocrine glands, capillaries and blood for endocrine glands.

**Apply the criteria to the observation.** No duct is present, so the secretion cannot be channelled to an epithelial surface; a very rich capillary network is exactly the feature the unit describes in endocrine glands.
**Conclude.** The gland is endocrine and its secretion consists of hormones released into the blood for systemic transport.

questions.q: A patient in Asmara has a blood sample analysed after a meal and again after an overnight fast. Complete the following paragraph by supplying the missing terms. After a meal, the beta cells of the pancreatic islets release (1) ______, which facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue and promotes the storage of glucose as glycogen, a process called (2) ______. During fasting, the alpha cells release (3) ______, which acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and (4) ______, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.
why: **Identify the postprandial hormone and its source.** The unit states that beta cells of the islets of Langerhans produce insulin, which facilitates glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states and lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake and glycogenesis.
**Name the storage process.** The conversion of absorbed glucose into stored glycogen is termed glycogenesis, so blank (2) is glycogenesis.
**Identify the fasting hormone.** Alpha cells of the same islets synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, acting principally on liver tissue.

**Name the second hepatic route to glucose.** Besides breaking glycogen down (glycogenolysis), glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, which fills blank (4).
**State the completed paragraph.** (1) insulin, (2) glycogenesis, (3) glucagon, (4) gluconeogenesis.

The outer region of the adrenal gland, called the (1) ______, secretes steroid corticosteroids such as cortisol and aldosterone, whereas the inner region, called the (2) ______, produces the amine catecholamines (3) ______ and norepinephrine that orchestrate the fight-or-flight response.

questions.q: A clinical laboratory in Asmara measures the effect of two pancreatic hormones on isolated liver hepatocytes. Explain how insulin and glucagon exert opposing effects on blood glucose concentration, and state the two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose.
questions.answer: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake into muscle, adipose tissue and liver and by promoting glycogenesis; glucagon raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in liver tissue, making the two hormones antagonistic.
why: **State the source and trigger of each hormone.** Within the islets of Langerhans, beta cells secrete insulin during postprandial (fed) states, while alpha cells secrete glucagon during fasting, so the two hormones are released under opposite physiological conditions.

**Describe the action of insulin on hepatocytes.** Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, that is, the conversion of glucose into stored glycogen in the liver; it also facilitates glucose transport into skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

**Describe the action of glucagon on hepatocytes.** Glucagon acts on liver tissue to raise blood glucose. It stimulates glycogenolysis, the breakdown of stored glycogen back into glucose, and gluconeogenesis, the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources.

**Explain why the pair is described as antagonistic.** Because insulin drives glucose out of the blood into storage while glucagon mobilises glucose from storage into the blood, the two hormones produce opposite net movements of glucose and therefore hold blood glucose within its narrow physiological range.

**Summarise the answer.** Insulin promotes cellular glucose uptake and glycogenesis (lowering blood glucose); glucagon promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver (raising blood glucose). The two processes by which glucagon raises blood glucose are glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

Together they maintain homeostasis because insulin lowers blood glucose during postprandial states (cellular uptake and glycogenesis), while glucagon raises it during fasting (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis).
why: **Correct the cell assignment.** The unit states that alpha cells synthesize and secrete glucagon to elevate blood glucose during fasting, while beta cells produce insulin to facilitate glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissues during postprandial states, so two distinct cell populations are involved.
**State the glucose-lowering arm.** Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular intake of glucose and by promoting glycogenesis, the storage of glucose as glycogen.
**State the glucose-raising arm.** Glucagon acts on liver tissue, stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to release glucose into the blood during fasting.

**Explain the homeostatic outcome.** Because the two hormones are released in opposite nutritional states and drive glucose in opposite directions, their balance keeps blood glucose within tight physiological bounds.

questions.q:
A 50 kg woman in Asmara is diagnosed with myxoedema and is prescribed thyroxine replacement at a dose of 3.4 micrograms per kilogram of body mass, given once daily. Each 200-microgram tablet costs 0.40 Nakfa.
(a) Calculate her daily thyroxine dose in micrograms.
(b) Express this daily dose in milligrams.
(c) Calculate the total cost in Nakfa of her thyroxine supply for 30 days.
(d) State the endocrine reason why she must take thyroxine, and explain what will happen to her blood TSH level while the treatment is adequate.
questions.answer: (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for a 30-day supply; (d) the thyroxine must be supplied because of hyposecretion of thyroxine (myxoedema), and once the dose restores normal thyroxine the negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary reduces the blood TSH level back towards normal.
why: **Identify the given data and the relation needed.** Body mass = 50 kg; dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg per day; tablet content = 200 micrograms; tablet cost = 0.40 Nakfa; duration = 30 days. The daily dose equals the dose per kilogram multiplied by body mass. The unit notes that hormones act in minute quantities measured in micrograms or picograms, so microgram units are appropriate here.
**Calculate the daily dose in micrograms.** Daily dose = 3.4 micrograms per kg x 50 kg = 170 micrograms per day.
**Convert micrograms to milligrams.** Since 1 milligram = 1000 micrograms, divide by 1000: 170 micrograms per day / 1000 = 0.17 milligram per day.

**Calculate the 30-day supply and its cost.** Total mass required = 170 micrograms per day x 30 days = 5100 micrograms = 5.1 milligrams. Cost = 5.1 milligrams x 0.40 Nakfa per milligram = 2.04 Nakfa for the 30-day supply.

**Give the endocrine explanation.** Myxoedema is caused by hyposecretion of thyroxine in an adult, and because thyroxine is the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, the missing hormone must be supplied from outside. Thyroxine normally exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary; when the replacement dose restores a normal circulating thyroxine concentration, that feedback is re-established and the pituitary stops over-secreting TSH, so blood TSH falls back towards normal.

**State the final results.** (a) 170 micrograms per day; (b) 0.17 milligram per day; (c) 2.04 Nakfa for 30 days; (d) thyroxine replacement is required because the gland hyposecretes the hormone, and adequate treatment suppresses the previously elevated blood TSH back to normal through negative feedback.

**Cost the 60-day supply.** Total mass = 150 micrograms per day x 60 days = 9000 micrograms = 9.0 milligrams. Cost = 9.0 milligrams x 0.50 Nakfa per milligram = 4.50 Nakfa.

**Test whole-tablet amounts.** One tablet provides 200 micrograms, which exceeds 136 micrograms by 64 micrograms, so it is the smallest whole-tablet dose that covers the requirement and is the practical choice; any smaller whole number of tablets gives zero micrograms.

questions.q:
A 70 kg fisherman from Massawa is diagnosed with hyperthyroidism caused by Graves' disease, and his basal metabolic rate is measured at 168 percent of the value expected for a healthy man of his age and body mass. His expected normal basal metabolic rate is 6800 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy in kJ per day that his body expends above the normal value.
(c) Express this excess as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Explain the endocrine basis of this raised metabolic rate and name the gland and the hormone responsible.
questions.answer: (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day of excess expenditure; (c) 68 percent above the normal basal metabolic rate; (d) the thyroid gland is hypersecreting thyroxine, and because thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, energy expenditure rises far above normal.
why: **Identify the given data and the principle.** Normal basal metabolic rate = 6800 kJ per day; measured rate = 168 percent of normal. Thyroxine is described in the unit as the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate, and hyperthyroidism accelerates metabolic rate to pathological levels.
**Calculate the actual basal metabolic rate.** Actual rate = 1.68 x 6800 kJ per day = 11,424 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess expenditure.** Excess = 11,424 kJ per day - 6800 kJ per day = 4624 kJ per day.

**Express the excess as a percentage.** Percentage excess = (4624 / 6800) x 100 percent = 0.68 x 100 percent = 68 percent, which agrees with the measured value being 68 percent above the normal 100 percent.

**Explain the endocrine mechanism.** The gland responsible is the thyroid gland, which is hypersecreting thyroxine. Thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, so an excess of thyroxine raises oxygen and fuel consumption above normal. This explains the unit's clinical picture of hyperthyroidism: rapid weight loss despite eating, heat intolerance, hyperactive reflexes and anxiety, together with chronic strain on the cardiovascular system from elevated heart rate and blood pressure.

**State the final results.** (a) 11,424 kJ per day; (b) 4624 kJ per day in excess; (c) 68 percent above normal; (d) hypersecretion of thyroxine by the thyroid gland elevates the basal metabolic rate of most somatic cells.

questions.q:
A 55 kg woman in Asmara with adult thyroxine hyposecretion has a basal metabolic rate measured at 82 percent of the value expected for a healthy woman of her age and body mass. Her expected normal rate is 5400 kJ per day.
(a) Calculate her actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the energy deficit in kJ per day relative to the normal value.
(c) Express this deficit as a percentage of the normal basal metabolic rate.
(d) Name the hormone that is deficient and explain why this reduces her basal metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 4428 kJ per day; (b) 972 kJ per day below normal; (c) 18 percent below normal; (d) thyroxine is deficient, and since thyroxine acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate and regulate heat production, its shortage lowers metabolism, matching the sluggish metabolism, weight gain and cold sensitivity of myxoedema.
why: **Convert the percentage to a multiplier.** A rate at 82 percent of normal corresponds to a multiplying factor of 0.82 applied to the normal value of 5400 kJ per day.
**Calculate the actual rate.** 0.82 x 5400 kJ per day = 4428 kJ per day.
**Calculate the deficit.** Deficit = 5400 kJ per day - 4428 kJ per day = 972 kJ per day.
**Express the deficit as a percentage.** (972 / 5400) x 100 percent = 18 percent, consistent with 100 percent - 82 percent = 18 percent.

**Explain the endocrine cause.** The deficient hormone is thyroxine, the primary regulator of basal metabolic rate. With less thyroxine acting on most somatic cells, heat production and metabolic rate fall, producing the low metabolic rate, weight gain and cold sensitivity characteristic of myxoedema.

questions.q:
A 16-year-old boy in Keren with a pituitary tumour has a basal metabolic rate measured at 120 percent of the normal value for his age and body mass, his normal rate being 6000 kJ per day. The tumour is hypersecreting Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH).
(a) Calculate his actual basal metabolic rate in kJ per day.
(b) Calculate the excess energy expended per day.
(c) Express the excess as a percentage of the normal rate.
(d) Explain the full chain of events from the pituitary tumour to the raised metabolic rate.
questions.answer: (a) 7200 kJ per day; (b) 1200 kJ per day in excess; (c) 20 percent above normal; (d) excess TSH from the tumour over-stimulates the thyroid gland, which synthesizes and releases excess thyroxine; thyroxine then acts on most somatic cells to elevate the basal metabolic rate, raising energy expenditure by 20 percent.
why: **Calculate the actual rate.** 1.20 x 6000 kJ per day = 7200 kJ per day.
**Calculate the excess.** Excess = 7200 kJ per day - 6000 kJ per day = 1200 kJ per day.
**Express the excess as a percentage.** (1200 / 6000) x 100 percent = 20 percent, consistent with 120 percent - 100 percent = 20 percent.

**Trace the hormonal chain.** TSH has the thyroid gland as its principal target tissue and stimulates the synthesis and release of thyroxine, so a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour drives thyroxine secretion upward.

**Link thyroxine to metabolism.** Thyroxine's target is most somatic cells, where it elevates the basal metabolic rate and regulates heat production; the excess hormone therefore accounts for the measured 20 percent rise in energy expenditure.

questions.q: A health educator at the hospital in Keren traces the route followed by sperm from the site of their formation to the point where they leave the male body through the urethra. According to the unit's SEVEN UP pathway, how many structures does a spermatozoon pass through during this journey, and what are they in order?

options.A: 4 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, urethra
options.B: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, penis
options.C: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, penis
options.D: 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

why: **Recall the SEVEN UP acronym.** The memory aid SEVEN UP gives the path of sperm: S = Seminiferous tubules, E = Epididymis, V = Vas deferens, E = Ejaculatory duct, N = Nothing (a placeholder, not a structure), U = Urethra, P = Penis. Only the six lettered structures carry sperm; the N entry is a memory aid with no anatomical counterpart.

**Check each structure against its stated role.** Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis; the epididymis stores spermatozoa and allows them to acquire motility; the vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum and loops over the urinary bladder; the ejaculatory duct is where the vas deferens joins; the urethra is the final tube; and the penis delivers semen.

**Reject the distractor pathways.** Options A and B place the vas deferens before the epididymis, but sperm enter the epididymis directly from the tubules and only later are propelled into the vas deferens. Options B and C omit the ejaculatory duct, which the unit explicitly lists between the vas deferens and the urethra. Options A and C also stop at the urethra and drop the penis.
**Count and conclude.** Six lettered structures remain once the placeholder N is excluded, giving the order seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

questions.q: A clinical technician in Asmara records a man's core body temperature as $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The unit states that spermatogenesis cannot occur effectively at core body temperature, and that the scrotum maintains an optimal microenvironment approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core body temperature. Calculate the full optimal scrotal temperature range, then state which of the following scrotal measurements would fall inside that range: $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ or $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
questions.answer: Optimal scrotal range = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$; the only measurement inside this range is $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
why: **State the governing principle.** The scrotum holds the testes outside the pelvic cavity so that sperm production occurs several degrees below core temperature, because high temperatures degrade the key germinal enzymes needed for spermatogenesis. The permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.
**Compute the upper end of the range.** The upper end is only $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compute the lower end of the range.** The lower end is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The optimal range is therefore $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ inclusive.

**Test each candidate measurement.** Compare each value with the interval $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C} \leq T \leq 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. For $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference from core is $$4.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which lies between $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ and $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it is inside. For $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference is only $$2.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; for $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$1.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; and for $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$0.8^{\circ}\text{C}$$. All three are less than $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature and therefore lie above $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, outside the range.
**Conclude.** The optimal scrotal temperature range is $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and of the four measurements only $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ falls within it.

Under warm conditions the dartos and cremaster muscles relax to promote heat loss, which drives the testes toward this cool end.

**Substitute the core temperature.** Using core body temperature $$= 37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, the extreme cool testicular temperature is $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**State the cooling differential.** Subtracting the testicular temperature from the core temperature gives $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 32.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so the testes are held $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

questions.q: A man in Asmara takes a prolonged hot bath and his scrotal temperature rises to $$36.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ while his core temperature remains $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. **Conclude.** The hot bath leaves the testes only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, which fails the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential, so sperm production is impaired.

questions.q: At a reproductive health session in Keren, a facilitator explains that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of the total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$, with the remainder coming from the bulbourethral glands and the spermatozoa themselves. If a single ejaculation has a total volume of $$3.0\text{ mL}$$, calculate the volume contributed by the seminal vesicles, the volume contributed by the prostate gland, and the combined volume contributed by all remaining sources.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.8\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.9\text{ mL}$$; all remaining sources $$= 0.3\text{ mL}$$ (together these sum to the $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ total).
why: **Identify the known quantities.** Total semen volume $$= 3.0\text{ mL}$$. Seminal vesicle contribution $$= 60\%$$ of total. Prostate gland contribution $$= 30\%$$ of total. The bulbourethral glands and spermatozoa account for whatever remains.

**Calculate the seminal vesicle volume.** Multiply the total volume by the seminal vesicle fraction: $$0.60 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 1.8\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid supplies fructose as metabolic fuel for sperm and prostaglandins that trigger contractions in the female reproductive tract, which is consistent with this gland providing the bulk of semen volume.

**Calculate the prostate gland volume.** Multiply the total volume by the prostate fraction: $$0.30 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.9\text{ mL}$$. This thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid contains citric acid and proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

**Calculate the remaining volume.** First find the remaining percentage: $$100\% - 60\% - 30\% = 10\%$$. Then apply it: $$0.10 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.3\text{ mL}$$. This residue corresponds to the clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands together with the spermatozoa.
**Check the total.** Add the parts: $$1.8\text{ mL} + 0.9\text{ mL} + 0.3\text{ mL} = 3.0\text{ mL}$$, which matches the stated total volume, so the calculation is consistent.

questions.q: A man in Massawa has been unable to conceive with his partner for two years. Semen analysis shows that sperm are being produced in normal numbers but almost all of them are immotile and none has acquired fertilizing capability, while the man's reproductive hormone levels are normal. Using only the structures and functions described in this unit, identify the single structure whose function is most likely impaired, and justify your answer with two functions of that structure.
questions.answer: The epididymis. It normally stores spermatozoa and provides the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability; normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm point to failure of exactly these two functions.
why: **Note that sperm production itself is intact.** The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis and the Sertoli cells provide nutrients and structural support to developing germ cells. Because sperm are produced in normal numbers, this function is clearly not the problem. The acrosome, which carries the hydrolytic enzymes needed to digest the egg's protective layers, is also formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, so the production line is working.

**Identify which function is missing.** The two missing features are motility and fertilizing capability. The unit states that sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability during their residence in the epididymis, where they undergo biochemical maturation over several weeks.

**Match the missing functions to the correct structure.** The epididymis is the crescent-shaped tubule coiled on the superior-posterior margin of each testis in which spermatozoa reside for several weeks. Its two functions are (i) storing spermatozoa and (ii) facilitating the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability. An impairment of this structure explains normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm.

**Confirm that the other ducts are not implicated.** The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular duct that simply transports mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct; it does not mature sperm. The unit also notes that mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens only during sexual arousal, whereas the immotility described here is a property of the sperm themselves, present regardless of arousal.

**Conclude.** The impaired structure is the epididymis, because the sperm have normal production but lack precisely the two properties, motility and fertilizing capability, that the epididymis confers during maturation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man in Asmara undergoes a vasectomy in which the vas deferens is cut and sealed. His testes continue to produce sperm and his Leydig cells continue to secrete testosterone. Explain, using only the unit's description of the male tract and of semen composition, what happens to the sperm produced after the operation and why the operation does not reduce his testosterone levels.
questions.answer: Sperm are still produced in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis, but they can no longer pass beyond the sealed vas deferens, so they are not included in the ejaculate; testosterone is unaffected because it is secreted by the Leydig cells, which the unit places under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary, not under the control of the vas deferens.
why: **Locate the cut in the pathway.** The vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that carries mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis out of the scrotum, through the inguinal canal and over the urinary bladder to the ejaculatory duct. Sealing it blocks this single transport route.

**Trace the fate of the sperm.** Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is unaffected, and sperm still pass into the epididymis to mature. However, they cannot be propelled beyond the blocked vas deferens, so no sperm reach the ejaculatory duct and urethra and none appear in the ejaculate, which is why vasectomy is a permanent surgical contraceptive method.

**Locate the source of testosterone.** In the interstitial space between adjacent seminiferous tubules lie the Leydig cells, which synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone from the anterior pituitary. These cells are entirely separate from the vas deferens.

**Explain why testosterone is unchanged.** Because the Leydig cells and the HPG axis that regulates them are untouched by the operation, testosterone secretion continues normally. Only the sperm delivery route, not the endocrine function of the testis, has been interrupted.

**Conclude.** After vasectomy, sperm are produced and matured but can no longer leave the tract, while testosterone levels remain normal because Leydig cells under LH control continue to secrete androgen independently of the vas deferens.

questions.q: A student in Keren claims that because the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release a clear fluid before ejaculation, that fluid must be the main carrier of sperm. Explain, using the unit's description of the male accessory glands, why this claim is incorrect, and state the two functions the bulbourethral glands actually perform.
questions.answer: The claim is incorrect because the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small clear, viscous pre-ejaculatory mucus; the bulk of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles (about 60%) and the prostate gland (about 30%). Their two functions are lubricating the urethra and neutralizing residual acidic urine prior to ejaculation.
why: **Establish the actual volume contributions.** The unit states that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$. Together these two glands account for about $$90\%$$ of semen, leaving only roughly $$10\%$$ for the bulbourethral gland secretion and the spermatozoa themselves.

**Show why the student's claim fails.** A secretion that forms only a small fraction of the ejaculate cannot be its main carrier of sperm. The spermatozoa themselves are the cellular component, suspended in the fluid vehicle formed mainly by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

**State the real functions of the bulbourethral glands.** The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus whose functions are to lubricate the urethra and to neutralize residual acidic urine before semen passes. These are preparatory and protective roles, not a sperm-carrying role.

questions.q: A man's blood testosterone level rises well above its normal stable value. Applying the negative feedback loop described in this unit, which of the following correctly states the resulting changes?

options.A: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to increase GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so testosterone production rises further.
options.B: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.
options.C: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion but on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so the two effects cancel and testosterone production is unchanged.
options.D: Testosterone acts directly on the seminiferous tubules to decrease spermatogenesis, and the reduced sperm numbers feed back on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release.

why: **Identify the axis being regulated.** Testosterone secretion is governed by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), which drives the anterior pituitary to release LH, and LH stimulates the Leydig cells of the testis to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

**State the direction of a negative feedback loop.** In negative feedback, a rise in the level of the final hormone in the chain suppresses the earlier steps of the chain. The unit states explicitly that as blood testosterone levels rise, testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, stabilizing hormone levels.

**Evaluate each option.** Option A describes positive feedback, in which rising testosterone would further increase GnRH and LH, which contradicts the stabilizing negative feedback the unit describes; it also misstates the effect on both organs. Option C is internally inconsistent, since the unit gives decreases at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. Option D introduces a sperm-count feedback signal that the unit never describes, and the unit's loop is defined by blood testosterone acting on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, not on the seminiferous tubules.

**Confirm the correct option and its consequence.** Option B matches the unit exactly: decreased GnRH and decreased LH. With less LH reaching the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells are less stimulated, testosterone secretion falls, and the elevated blood level is brought back down toward its stable value.
**Conclude.** Rising blood testosterone suppresses the HPG axis at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so option B is the correct statement of the feedback response.

questions.q: A laboratory report for a patient in Asmara shows a very low blood testosterone level together with an abnormally high LH level, and the hypothalamic GnRH secretion is found to be high. Which single structure does this pattern indicate is failing, and what is the normal response of that structure to LH?
questions.answer: The Leydig cells (interstitial cells) of the testis are failing. Normally LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, so unrepaired Leydig cells should raise testosterone output when LH is high.
why: **Read the pattern of hormones.** GnRH is high and LH is high, so the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary are both sending strong stimulatory signals down the HPG axis. The defect therefore lies below the pituitary.

**Identify the target of LH.** The unit states that the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells lying between adjacent seminiferous tubules, synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone secreted from the anterior pituitary.

**Explain why high LH with low testosterone is diagnostic.** If the Leydig cells were responding normally, a high LH level would drive testosterone production upward. Instead testosterone remains very low, so the Leydig cells are not responding to LH stimulation and are the failing structure.

**Account for the high upstream hormones.** Because testosterone is the signal that suppresses the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, low testosterone removes that inhibition. GnRH and LH therefore remain high, which is exactly what the report shows.
**Conclude.** The failing structure is the Leydig cell population of the testis, whose normal response to LH is to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

questions.q: A man in Keren receives a treatment that keeps his blood testosterone concentration artificially high for several weeks. Predict the effect of this treatment on the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone and Luteinizing Hormone, and explain how the treatment will affect the activity of his Leydig cells.
questions.answer: GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus and LH release from the anterior pituitary will both decrease through negative feedback; with less LH stimulation the Leydig cells will become less active and their own testosterone secretion will fall.
why: **Recognise the feedback signal.** Blood testosterone is the final hormone of the HPG axis and acts as the inhibitory signal on the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. An artificially raised level therefore acts as a strong inhibitory signal.
**Predict the hypothalamic response.** The hypothalamus responds by decreasing its secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone, the hormone that normally drives the anterior pituitary.
**Predict the pituitary response.** The anterior pituitary responds to the raised testosterone directly, as well as to the reduced GnRH, by decreasing its release of Luteinizing Hormone.

**Trace the effect on Leydig cells.** Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testosterone when stimulated by LH. With LH release suppressed, the Leydig cells receive less stimulation and become less active, so the testis's own contribution to blood testosterone declines even while the external treatment maintains a high total level.
**Conclude.** Sustained high blood testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH through negative feedback, and the reduced LH stimulation in turn lowers the secretory activity of the Leydig cells.

why: **Identify the composition fractions from the unit.** The unit states that the organic portion is approximately $$\frac{1}{3}$$ of total bone mass (collagen fibres, ground substance and bone cells) and that the inorganic mineral salts are the remaining $$\frac{2}{3}$$ (mainly calcium phosphate crystals in the form of hydroxyapatite).

**Calculate the mass of the inorganic mineral salts.** Inorganic mass = $$\frac{2}{3} \times 480\text{ g} = 320\text{ g}$$. Check: 160 g + 320 g = 480 g, which equals the total mass of the sample.

(a) Calculate the total number of individual ribs. (b) Calculate the percentage of the total ribs that are true ribs and the percentage that are floating ribs, each correct to one decimal place.
questions.answer: (a) There are 24 individual ribs. (b) True ribs = $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% \approx 58.3\%$$ and floating ribs = $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% \approx 16.7\%$$ of all ribs.
why: **Convert pairs of ribs into individual ribs.** 12 pairs of ribs = 12 $$\times$$ 2 = 24 individual ribs.
**Calculate the number of true ribs.** True ribs are the top 7 pairs, which connect directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilages: 7 $$\times$$ 2 = 14 ribs.
**Calculate the number of floating ribs.** Floating ribs are the bottom 2 pairs, which do not connect to the sternum at all: 2 $$\times$$ 2 = 4 ribs.

**Express each group as a percentage of 24 ribs.** True ribs: $$\frac{14}{24} \times 100\% = 58.333\ldots\% \approx 58.3\%$$. Floating ribs: $$\frac{4}{24} \times 100\% = 16.666\ldots\% \approx 16.7\%$$. The remaining 6 false ribs give $$\frac{6}{24} \times 100\% = 25.0\%$$, and 58.3% + 25.0% + 16.7% = 100%.

questions.q: A cyclist riding from Asmara down to Massawa falls from her bicycle and injures her knee. At the hospital the doctor explains that the knee is a freely movable joint. (a) Describe the structural features of a freely movable (synovial) joint and explain how these features prevent wear and tear on the articulating bone ends during high-impact movement. (b) Classify the elbow joint, the shoulder joint and the atlas-axis joint by their mechanical shape, and state the movement that each one permits.
questions.answer: (a) In a synovial joint the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with synovial fluid and enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane. Articular (hyaline) cartilage cushions the bone ends and absorbs compressional shock, while the synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, so wear and tear are prevented. (b) The elbow is a hinge joint (flexion and extension in a single plane), the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint (multidirectional rotation), and the atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint (rotation around a central axis).
why: **Define the freely movable joint.** A freely movable (synovial) joint is one in which the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, and the whole joint is enclosed by a tough articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**Explain the role of articular cartilage.** The bone ends are covered by a layer of articular (hyaline) cartilage. This cartilage cushions the bone ends, absorbs compressional shock and minimises friction between the moving surfaces.

**Explain the role of synovial fluid and the capsule.** The synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity; this slippery fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction to near zero, while the articular capsule holds the fluid in place and keeps the joint stable.
**Classify the elbow joint.** The elbow is a hinge joint, in which a convex surface fits into a concave depression, permitting flexion and extension in a single plane.

**Classify the shoulder and the atlas-axis joints.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, in which a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes. The atlas-axis joint is a pivot joint, in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation of the head around a central axis.

questions.q: A metalworker in Asmara can swing his arm freely in all directions, yet the bones of his skull cannot move at all. Compare the skull sutures and the shoulder joint in terms of the connective tissue that binds the bones, the range of movement allowed, and the protective or mechanical advantage each arrangement provides.
questions.answer: The skull sutures are immovable (fibrous) joints, bound tightly by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue, allowing zero movement so that the delicate brain is protected. The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) ball-and-socket joint with a joint cavity, synovial fluid, an articular capsule and a synovial membrane, allowing rotational movement in multiple planes so that the arm can be used for mechanical work.
why: **Describe the immovable joint.** Immovable (fibrous) joints, such as the sutures of the skull, are bound together by dense, tough fibrous connective tissue and allow zero movement.
**State the advantage of the immovable joint.** Because no movement is possible, the fused skull bones form a rigid protective case for the delicate tissues of the brain.

**Describe the freely movable joint.** The shoulder is a freely movable (synovial) joint: the articulating bone ends are separated by a joint cavity filled with lubricating synovial fluid, enclosed by an articular capsule lined with a synovial membrane.

**State the mechanical advantage and conclude.** The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, so a ball-like head fits into a cup-like socket and rotational movement in multiple planes is possible. This gives the arm a wide range of movement for lifting and manipulating objects, whereas the skull sutures give protection instead of mobility.

questions.q: A long-distance bus driver in Keren complains of stiffness and pain in his back. Explain how the type of joint between the vertebrae allows the spine to be both flexible and shock-absorbing, and contrast this with the joint that allows the head to turn from side to side.
questions.answer: The vertebrae are joined by slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, which permit limited, restricted movement so the spine is flexible and the discs absorb shock. The side-to-side turning of the head is produced by the pivot joint between the atlas and the axis, which allows rotation around a central axis.
why: **Identify the joint between the vertebrae.** The 33 vertebrae are separated by fibrocartilaginous intervertebral discs, making these slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints that are connected by resilient pads of cartilage.
**Explain the movement and shock absorption.** Slightly movable joints permit only limited, restricted movement; this gives the spine flexibility while the discs absorb shock and provide stability.

**Identify the joint used for turning the head.** The first two cervical vertebrae form the atlas-axis joint, which is a pivot joint in which a rounded surface rotates within a ring, allowing rotation around a central axis.

**Contrast the two joint types and conclude.** The vertebral joints are cartilaginous and allow only slight movement distributed along the column, whereas the atlas-axis pivot joint allows full rotation of the head. Neither joint is a freely movable synovial joint of the ball-and-socket kind.

questions.q: A 13-year-old student in Keren is told by a doctor that the long bones of her arms and legs are still elongating. (a) Explain how endochondral ossification at the epiphyseal plates allows a long bone to increase in length, naming the cells and processes involved. (b) Explain why elongation stops at skeletal maturity. (c) The unit states that approximately 10% of the entire adult skeleton is completely replaced every year by bone remodeling. Deduce the number of years required for a complete turnover of the skeleton, and name the two cell types responsible for remodeling and state the role of each.
questions.answer: (a) The embryonic cartilage model is invaded by blood vessels that deliver osteoblasts, which replace cartilage with mineralised bone, while at the epiphyseal plate chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side and osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates. (b) Elongation stops because the epiphyseal plates completely ossify at skeletal maturity, leaving no cartilage to be converted into bone. (c) A complete turnover of the skeleton takes $$\frac{100\%}{10\%} = 10\text{ years}$$; the two cell types are osteoblasts (which build and mineralise bone matrix) and osteoclasts (which dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium).
why: **State the starting material of the embryonic skeleton.** During early fetal development the skeleton is composed almost entirely of flexible hyaline cartilage, and ossification is the process by which this embryonic cartilage is transformed into solid bone.

**Describe endochondral ossification.** In endochondral ossification, blood vessels invade the cartilage models and deliver osteoblasts, which gradually replace the cartilage with a hard mineralised matrix.

**Explain growth at the epiphyseal plate.** In children the epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones. Chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate, while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone elongates.

**Explain why growth stops at skeletal maturity.** The plates continue to allow elongation only until they completely ossify at skeletal maturity. Once the plate has ossified there is no cartilage left for the chondrocytes to divide and for the osteoblasts to replace, so the bone can no longer increase in length.
**Calculate the time for complete skeletal turnover.** If 10% of the skeleton is replaced each year, then the time for a complete turnover is $$\frac{100\%}{10\%\text{ per year}} = 10\text{ years}$$.

**Name the remodeling cells and their roles.** Osteoblasts are bone-building cells that synthesise and deposit the organic osteoid matrix and facilitate its mineralisation. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated bone-resorbing cells that secrete acids and enzymes to dissolve bone minerals and digest collagen, releasing calcium into the blood.

questions.q: A 15-year-old boy in Massawa fractures the shaft of his femur while playing football, and the doctor says the bone will heal rapidly. Explain why bone heals much faster than cartilage following physical trauma, referring to the blood supply and cells of each tissue.
questions.answer: Bone heals rapidly because it is highly vascular: the periosteum is rich in blood vessels and contains bone-forming osteoblasts, and the central canals and perforating canals deliver nutrients and cells directly to the injury site. Cartilage is entirely avascular and must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding perichondrium, so it heals much more slowly.
why: **Describe the blood supply and cells of bone.** The unit states that the outer surface of a bone is covered by the periosteum, a fibrous membrane rich in blood vessels, nerves and bone-forming stem cells called osteoblasts, and that central canals and perforating canals carry vessels into the bone.

**Link this to rapid repair.** Because nutrients and osteoblasts are delivered directly to the fracture site by the rich blood supply, the bone matrix can be rebuilt quickly, which is why a fractured femur shaft heals rapidly.

**Describe the blood supply of cartilage.** Cartilage is entirely avascular (lacking blood vessels), so it must rely on slow nutrient diffusion from the surrounding tissues (perichondrium) to repair itself.

**Conclude the comparison.** The absence of a direct blood supply makes cartilage repair slow, whereas the highly vascular periosteum, central canals and perforating canals of bone make bone repair comparatively rapid.

questions.q: A child in Asmara suffers a disorder in which the epiphyseal plates of the long bones ossify completely at the age of 8 years instead of at skeletal maturity. Predict the effect on the length of the child's arms and legs, and explain the role of the growth plate in normal bone elongation, naming the cells involved.
questions.answer: The arms and legs will stop elongating at 8 years and the child will remain unusually short, because the epiphyseal plates have ossified and no cartilage remains. Normally chondrocytes divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side, so the bone keeps elongating until the plate ossifies at skeletal maturity.
why: **Recall the normal role of the epiphyseal plate.** The epiphyseal plates (growth plates) lie between the shaft and the ends of long bones; chondrocytes continuously divide on the cartilage side of the plate while osteoblasts replace the old cartilage with bone on the osseous side.
**Relate the plate to elongation.** This continuous division and replacement is what allows bones to elongate during childhood, so the arms and legs grow longer year by year.

**Apply the premature ossification.** If the plates ossify completely at 8 years, there is no cartilage left for chondrocytes to divide and no cartilage for osteoblasts to replace, so elongation of the long bones ceases permanently.

**State the predicted outcome.** The child's arms and legs will stop growing at 8 years and remain short, so the child will be unusually short, whereas normally elongation continues until the plates ossify at skeletal maturity.

cards.title: 5.3.1 The Pancreas and its Hormones
body: The pancreas secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon to control the level of glucose in the blood.

The insulin also sends signal to the liver to convert glucose into the glucosereserve known as glycogen.

cards.title: 5.3.2 The Liver and Sugar Control
body: The liver acts as a storehouse for glycogen.

cards.q: Which of the following describes the double fertilization event in angiosperms?

options.A: Two sperm cells fertilize two separate egg cells to produce fraternal twins.
options.B: One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.
options.C: One sperm fertilizes the ovary wall, while the second sperm forms the seed coat.
options.D: Two pollen tubes fertilize the same egg to produce a diploid endosperm.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Review angiosperm reproductive events**
Angiosperms undergo a unique double fertilization process utilizing two sperm nuclei from a single pollen tube.

**Step 2: Trace both fertilization pathways**
One sperm ($$n$$) fertilizes the egg ($$n$$) to form a zygote ($$2n$$). The second sperm ($$n$$) fuses with the two polar nuclei ($$n+n$$) to form the triploid endosperm ($$3n$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One sperm fertilizes the egg to form a zygote, while the second sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm.**

**Step 1: Review water transport models**
Water moves up tall plants under negative pressure (tension).

**Step 2: Name the primary model**
The cohesion-tension theory explains that water is pulled up by transpiration, held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion), and supported by xylem walls (adhesion).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **Cohesion-tension theory**.
